articles.title: Datafolha: mais de 80% mantêm voto em presidente após crise no STF | G1
articles.standfirst: 85% não mudaram o voto após revelação de conversas entre Moraes e Vorcaro, e 86% mantiveram candidato após pedido de investigação contra Mendonça. STF discute caso na terça (15).
articles.summary: Datafolha aponta que a crise no STF entre Alexandre de Moraes e André Mendonça não alterou a intenção de voto de mais de 80% dos brasileiros.
articles.body:
Na imagem, ministros do STF: Alexandre de Moraes (dir.) e André Mendonça — Foto: Fotos de: Fabio Rodrigues-Pozzebom da Agência Brasil e Carlos Moura do STF

Pesquisa Datafolha divulgada neste sábado (12) mediu o impacto da crise no Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) na eleição do próximo presidente do Brasil.

Segundo o levantamento, 85% disseram que não mudaram de voto após ficarem sabendo da troca de mensagens entre Daniel Vorcaro, ex-dono do Banco Master, e o ministro Alexandre de Moraes . Outros 7% não mudaram, mas ficaram em dúvida. Os que mudaram o voto e os que não sabem tiveram a mesma proporção: 4% cada.

A revelação das conversas entre Vorcaro e Moraes:

Mudou de ideia sobre o voto para presidente: 4%

Resultado similar teve o impacto do requerimento de Alexandre de Moraes que, por sua vez, pediu para que o ministro André Mendonça fosse investigado. O ministro se baseou em relatórios de inteligência da PF que não possuem 'valor probatório.'

Neste caso, 86% dos entrevistados disseram não ter mudado o voto para presidente ao saber do pedido de investigação. Outros 7% não mudaram, mas ficaram em dúvida. 2% alteraram o candidato a presidente e 4% disseram não saber.

O pedido de investigação de Mendonça após suspeita levantada por Moraes:

Mudou de ideia sobre o voto para presidente: 2%

Em outra questão abordada pelo Datafolha, 71% afirmam concordar que o STF é essencial para proteger a democracia no Brasil. Outros 21% discordam e 3% não concordam nem discordam. Por fim, 5% não souberam responder.

A pesquisa foi encomendada pelo jornal Folha de S.Paulo e pela Globo. O Datafolha ouviu 2.002 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais entre os dias 8 e 10 de setembro. A margem de erro é de 2 pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%. O número de registro no TSE é BR-01833/2026.

Crise no STF se intensificou nas últimas semanas

A crise no Supremo Tribunal Federal se intensificou após a divulgação de um relatório da Polícia Federal (PF) produzido no âmbito do caso do banco Master.

Tornado público em 1º de setembro por decisão do ministro André Mendonça, relator do caso no STF, o documento reúne mensagens enviadas pelo ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro a um contato atribuído pelos investigadores ao ministro Alexandre de Moraes , além de referências a encontros e pedidos de orientação e proteção diante do avanço das investigações.

Os ministros do STF Edson Fachin, André Mendonça, Flávio Dino e Alexandre de Moraes — Foto: Alejandro Zambrana/STF, Antonio Augusto/STF e Gustavo Moreno/STF

Parte das mensagens foi trocada nos dias anteriores à primeira prisão de Vorcaro, em novembro de 2025. Como o material foi extraído do celular do ex-banqueiro, o relatório não contém eventuais respostas de Moraes.

A Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) pediu a nulidade do documento , e o plenário do Supremo deverá decidir sobre os próximos passos.

O conflito ganhou nova dimensão em 3 de setembro. Com base em relatórios internos de inteligência da PF, Moraes sustentou haver indícios de irregularidades na atuação de Mendonça, citando, em tese, improbidade administrativa, abuso de autoridade, crime de responsabilidade e possível favorecimento político na condução de apurações relacionadas aos casos Master e INSS. Os documentos, porém, continham ressalvas de que não havia valor probatório nas informações.

Com base nesses elementos, Moraes pediu que Mendonça fosse investigado no inquérito das fake news , do qual era relator. Mendonça, por sua vez, afirmou ter sido alvo de monitoramento pela PF e apontou possíveis irregularidades na elaboração dos documentos usados contra ele. Depois, Fachin retirou esse pedido do inquérito das fake news e tirou de Moraes a relatoria .

Afastamento e reintegração de diretores da PF

A disputa também alcançou o comando da Polícia Federal. No dia 8, Mendonça determinou o afastamento do diretor-geral da PF, Andrei Rodrigues , e do diretor de Inteligência, Leandro Almada.

O ministro disse que a PF o submeteu a monitoramento ilegal. No dia seguinte, o ministro Flávio Dino determinou a reintegração de Rodrigues e Almada , em uma nova decisão, paralela à de Mendonça. Em seguida, o presidente do STF, Edson Fachin, suspendeu as duas medidas conflitantes — a de afastamento e a de reintegração —, o que manteve Andrei no cargo, e pediu explicações ao diretor-geral da PF.

Em manifestação enviada a Fachin nesta sexta-feira (11), Andrei Rodrigues negou que a PF tenha monitorado Mendonça e afirmou que os relatórios foram produzidos de forma regular pela área de inteligência da corporação e encaminhados a Moraes em cumprimento de ordem judicial.

Fachin convocou para terça-feira (15) uma sessão extraordinária do plenário para discutir o relatório da PF sobre as mensagens de Vorcaro a Moraes e o encaminhamento do caso. Além disso, determinou a abertura integral dos documentos vinculados ao Master sob a relatoria de Mendonça . O objetivo é assegurar que os ministros tenham acesso ao acervo antes da sessão.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro e Daniel Vorcaro: PF revela cronologia de contatos | G1
articles.standfirst: Relatório da PF aponta que senador atuou como interlocutor direto do banqueiro nas tratativas financeiras de filme sobre Jair Bolsonaro, com cobrança de parcelas e reuniões.
articles.summary: Relatório da PF detalha como Flávio Bolsonaro atuou na captação de recursos com Daniel Vorcaro para o filme sobre Jair Bolsonaro, incluindo cobranças de repasses.
articles.body:
A Polícia Federal listou uma série de encontros presenciais, ligações e trocas de mensagens diretas entre o senador Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL -RJ) e o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, dono Master.

Os dados constam em relatório da PF elaborado a partir da extração do celular de Vorcaro e de relatórios de inteligência financeira do Conselho de Controle de Atividades Financeiras (Coaf).

O documento está entre os materiais de inquéritos no Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) cujos sigilos foram retirados pelo ministro André Mendonça .

Segundo os investigadores, os elementos indicam que Flávio não atuou apenas como terceiro citado em negociações, mas sim como um interlocutor direto de Vorcaro para viabilizar aportes financeiros para a produção da cinebiografia do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro , obra intitulada "Dark Horse" .

Sobre essa apuração, Flávio Bolsonaro, após ter negado que havia pedido recursos a Vorcaro para a produção do filme , confirmou que solicitou verbas ao ex-banqueiro.

O candidato do PL à Presidência disse também que os contatos com Vorcaro fizeram parte de uma relação privada de captação de patrocínio. Ele negou ter recebido qualquer valor diretamente ou cometido irregularidades.

A PF aponta que a atuação do senador abrangeu desde a cobrança por repasses atrasados até reuniões presenciais e o acompanhamento próximo do cronograma das gravações.

De acordo com a linha do tempo montada pela PF, a relação direta entre o senador e o banqueiro intensificou-se no segundo semestre de 2025:

20 de agosto de 2025 : primeiro registro direto de troca de mensagens entre Daniel Vorcaro e Flávio Bolsonaro. O banqueiro combina um horário ("21 pode ser") e Flávio responde afirmativamente, informando às 21h47 que estava "a caminho", indicando um encontro presencial, segundo os investigadores.

8 de setembro de 2025 : Flávio envia um áudio a Vorcaro cobrando os repasses em atraso para o filme. O senador expressa receio com a inadimplência e o risco de dar "calote" em figuras prestigiadas do cinema norte-americano, citando nominalmente o ator protagonista Jim Caviezel, que interpreta Jair Bolsonaro, e o diretor Cyrus Nowrasteh. Vorcaro responde pedindo desculpas pela situação e promete resolver no dia seguinte.

15 de setembro de 2025 : o empresário Thiago Miranda avisa a Vorcaro que Flávio queria encontrá-lo pessoalmente para mostrar o material gravado, propondo uma reunião na residência do banqueiro em Brasília. Vorcaro concorda.

16 de setembro de 2025 : registro de ligação telefônica entre Vorcaro e Flávio Bolsonaro. A data coincide exatamente com a última remessa financeira de US$ 1,66 milhão realizada pela Entre Investimentos para a Havengate Development Fund nos Estados Unidos, conforme apurado pelo Coaf.

17 de setembro de 2025 : nova troca de mensagens entre o senador e o banqueiro sugere a realização de mais uma reunião presencial ("14:30?"). Tentativas adicionais de agendamento presencial ocorreram nos dias 23 e 24 do mesmo mês.

22 de outubro de 2025 : Flávio alerta Vorcaro de que o projeto já se encontrava no terceiro dia de filmagens e que a produção estava "no limite" orçamentário. O parlamentar pede que, caso o aporte não fosse viabilizado, o banqueiro avisasse imediatamente para que ele pudesse encontrar "outro caminho com urgência". No mesmo dia, Vorcaro responde que iria ver o assunto e que havia liberado mais uma parcela. Em seguida, Flávio o convida para um jantar em São Paulo com Jim Caviezel e Cyrus Nowrasteh.

Final de outubro e início de novembro de 2025 : Thiago Miranda volta a interpelar o banqueiro, alertando que os pagamentos supostamente efetuados não haviam chegado aos destinatários no exterior.

7 de novembro de 2025 : Flávio encaminha um vídeo da produção a Vorcaro com mensagem de agradecimento, dizendo que o filme só estaria sendo concretizado em virtude do apoio dele: "Tá perdendo, irmão! Tudo isso só está sendo possível por causa de vc!".

16 de novembro de 2025 : às vésperas da ação policial, Flávio tenta ligação e encaminha mensagens a Vorcaro: "Irmão, estou e estarei contigo sempre, não tem meia conversa entre a gente. Só preciso que me dê uma luz! Abs!". O banqueiro reage com imagem de visualização única e Flávio finaliza com "Amém".

17 de novembro de 2025 : por volta das 22h, Daniel Vorcaro é preso pela PF ao tentar embarcar em jato particular com destino ao exterior. Na manhã seguinte, a PF deflagra a primeira fase da Operação Compliance Zero.

Não está no relatório da PF, mas, em maio deste ano, veio à tona a informação de que Flávio Bolsonaro se encontrou com Vorcaro quando o ex-banqueiro estava preso em regime domiciliar, utilizando tornozeleira eletrônica no fim de 2025.

Flávio Bolsonaro admitiu que se encontrou com o ex-dono do Master entre a primeira e a segunda prisões de Vorcaro . Segundo o senador do PL, a reunião serviu para para "botar ponto final na questão" do filme "Dark Horse".

Nas investigações, os agentes federais destacam que a dinâmica apurada exige aprofundamento das apurações para esclarecer cinco pontos centrais .

origem dos recursos : de onde partiram os valores para subsidiar o filme;

empresas intermediárias : o motivo do uso da empresa Entre Investimentos e Participações, ligada ao empresário Antônio Carlos Freixo Júnior , o "Mineiro", como ponte dos recursos;

fundos nos EUA : qual a real função exercida pelo fundo Havengate Development Fund LP, registrado no Texas.

beneficiários finais : quem de fato recebeu os valores remetidos ao exterior;

divisão de papéis : a função concreta de Flávio Bolsonaro, de seu irmão o deputado Eduardo Bolsonaro (PL-SP), do deputado federal Mario Frias (PL-RJ), do empresário Thiago Miranda, de Fabiano Zettel (cunhado de Vorcaro), de Antônio Freixo e dos operadores do fundo norte-americano, Altieres Santana e Paulo Calixto, na captação, gestão e destino das quantias.

Flávio Bolsonaro tem declarado publicamente que o financiamento da produção se tratou de uma relação privada de captação de patrocínio, negando ter recebido qualquer valor diretamente ou cometido irregularidades.

A defesa do senador vem defendendo a retirada integral do sigilo dos autos das investigações.

articles.title: Trump asks Smithsonian to install George Washington statues, exhibition
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump asked the Smithsonian Institution on Friday to install statues of George Washington, in his latest bid to reshape the treasured mus...
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump asked the Smithsonian Institution on Friday to install statues of George Washington, in his latest bid to reshape the treasured museum and research complex.

Trump, who has sought to root out what he called "woke" culture, has accused the Smithsonian -- which operates 21 museums and galleries --- of trying to rewrite American history on issues of race and gender.

A 162-page White House report said that Smithsonian leadership has "consistently denigrated and displaced whites, males, Christians, and Americans in educational materials and programming".

Trump called for the installation of a 30-foot (nine-meter) "Colossus statue" of George Washington, a founding father and the first US president, and an exhibition honoring his legacy at The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History in Washington.

Trump also said he wanted the 11-foot (three-meter) statue of Washington that featured in August's Freedom 250 IndyCar motor race to go on display in the museum's Flag Hall.

The president asked for a five-year exhibition continuing through February 22, 2032 -- the 300th anniversary of Washington's birth -- to honor his "Life and Legacy."

"He is easily America's Greatest Hero. Without him, our Country and our Freedoms wouldn't exist," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

"And yet, during our Nation's 250th Anniversary Year, the Museum has failed to give George Washington and our other Founding Fathers the celebration they deserve."

The Smithsonian was created by the federal government in 1846 but operates in a unique position outside any branch of government.

articles.title: JD Vance embraces tricky role as Trump’s midterm messenger — and potential successor
articles.summary: Behind closed doors on Thursday, Vice President JD Vance urged a room full of Republicans to sell voters on the administration’s more popular achievements th...
articles.body:
Behind closed doors on Thursday, Vice President JD Vance urged a room full of Republicans to sell voters on the administration's more popular achievements that he worried weren't always breaking through.

One person, however, has proved particularly difficult to keep on message: President Donald Trump.

Since joining Trump's ticket in 2024, Vance has taken on the role of disciplined translator for a president whose instinct-driven improvisational style enthralls his admirers but often pulls attention from the message his advisers want voters to hear. Now, with control of Congress at stake in November , that role has taken new urgency. Vance is expected to aggressively campaign for Republican candidates — "divide and conquer" with Trump, as one source close to him put it — as the two carve up the midterm map.

The stakes for both Vance and the Republican Party will stretch beyond November, as he weighs his own future as the president's likeliest political heir.

Vance offered a telling example of his approach Thursday at an event outside Trump's two-day midterm convention in Dallas. According to audio obtained by CNN, Vance told convention attendees from his home state of Ohio and the battlegrounds of Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin that TrumpRx — a website for Americans to search for prescription drug discounts — was "the single issue that has the most broad, popular appeal."

"You see this in every poll that we've ever seen," Vance said.

Yet, Trump waited until the second hour of his midterm convention speech Wednesday to mention the initiative — and even then did not namecheck the program that bears his surname.

Vance had his own turn before the party faithful Thursday, headlining night two of the Republican Party's midterm convention (before Trump returned to the stage to close out the gathering). There, Vance playfully batted away chants of "JD! 48!" — a reference to the hope that he will succeed the 47th president — as premature, while sidestepping the topics that animated Trump's own remarks, like his surprise pledge to cut Americans $5,000 checks if his party holds power, the Iran war and tariffs.

Instead, he laid out a vision for Trump's America First movement focused on families and forgotten Americans that could serve as a platform for a presidential campaign. He also urged Republicans not to let differences divide them to the benefit of Democrats, as he continues a months-long push to keep Trump's fragile coalition together for the midterm elections and beyond.

"Don't give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there," he said.

The appearance served as a preview of how Vance intends to approach the final two months before Election Day. He'll be deployed on the trail in a similar fashion as 2024, when the campaign leaned into his relative youth and blue-collar roots to connect with young people, especially men, and Rust Belt workers.

The vice president has said he will wait until after the midterms to decide whether to run for president in 2028.

Tyler Bowyer, the chief operating officer at Turning Point Action, told CNN that he expects the outcome of the midterm elections "matters a whole lot" in Vance's calculus. Turning Point, a conservative organization founded by the assassinated activist Charlie Kirk, has endorsed Vance and is seen as a political operation in waiting for him if he wants it.

"If I was the vice president, I would want to see what the outcomes look like from November," Bowyer said. "Some of that you can control as the administration. Some of it you can't."

Already Vance is increasingly behaving like a politician with higher aspirations. He published his second book this summer on his Catholic faith and engaged in an extensive publicity tour that included sit-downs with "The View," conservative influencers and Christian media.

He is traveling, endorsing, and podcasting. He also moonlights as his party's finance chair, a role that conveniently puts him in front of GOP's deep-pocketed donors.

Inside the convention at the American Airlines Center, there was widespread recognition that Vance is the leading contender to become the party's 2028 nominee. Some are eager for Trump to declare it out loud.

"He truly gets the MAGA movement and all the parts of it," said AK Kamara, a Republican National Committeeman from Minnesota. "He's almost like the next iteration of what MAGA truly should be, which is, 'we have to be focused on America first.'"

But mention Vance and 2028 to Trump's supporters and another name often surfaces, sometimes unprompted: Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Though Rubio has publicly said he would support Vance if he runs, plenty of conservatives still view him as a shrewd, competent operator in Trump's Washington with presidential potential.

"I really favor somebody that's doing 12 jobs for the price of one," said Deanna Mclaughlin, who works in a Tennessee congressional office.

Republicans are also divided on how much say Trump should have in choosing who carries his movement forward. While McLaughlin said "the people need to decide," Rusat Ramgopal, executive director for the Queens County, New York, GOP said he hoped Trump, Rubio and Vance would work out the party's future together.

"It would be more beneficial to the party to not have the two biggest names duking it out in a primary," he said. "I think a unified ticket with those two, the biggest names in the party, will be a winning ticket in 2028."

In the near term, Vance remains one of Trump's closest advisers and most ardent public defenders, even as the White House navigates a Middle East war that the vice president had privately expressed reservations about from the start.

But in recent months, Vance has seized on his assignment to head an anti-fraud task force as an opportunity to carve out a more distinctive message in speeches around the country — as well as use the frequent travel to deepen ties with the GOP donors and party officials he'll need if he opts to run in 2028.

During those appearances, Vance has struck a more accommodating tone on the economy, eschewing Trump's blanket dismissals of voters' affordability concerns in favor of rhetoric that acknowledges Americans' frustration while simultaneously urging them to stay the course. Vance notably has expressed far more sympathy for voters' worries about data centers than Trump has.

The domestic tour has also allowed him to raise his public profile through focusing on anti-fraud issues that play well across the Republican Party, GOP operatives noted — rather than subjecting him to constant questions about the war in Iran.

"He connects uniquely," one Trump ally said of Vance. "He's a very approachable guy and appealing to a very important demographic in the Trump coalition."

Yet while Trump has continued to praise Vance in public and private, there's little expectation that the president will move any time soon to clear the 2028 field for him. Vance and his team will not only have to determine his path forward, but navigate Trump's own desire to cling to the spotlight as long as possible.

It was notable that Vance spoke on the final day of the two-night convention — and also that Trump appeared again right after him to close out the event.

"They can't move before the midterms," Curt Mills, executive director of "The American Conservative" and a Vance ally, said of his turn on the national stage. "The question is, is it a November decision, a February decision or a spring decision?"

CNN's Adam Cancryn, Kit Maher and Alayna Treene contributed to this report.

articles.title: White House unloads on violent ‘criminal alien’ nabbed after investigators uncover election offense
articles.summary: Anthony Tyrone Higgs, a Bahamian green card holder with a violent rap sheet, was arrested after officials say he illegally voted in the 2020 election.
articles.body: A Bahamian national who arrived in the U.S. during President Gerald Ford’s administration and was living with a green card racked up a violent rap sheet before investigators found he voted illegally in the 2020 election, sparking the deportation process, officials say. The case of Anthony Tyrone Higgs is only the latest in a slew of arrests connected to illegal votes cast in recent elections, as the Trump administration engages in a broader crackdown on election integrity-related crimes. "This alien was a guest in our country who forfeited his right to be in the U.S. when he committed these violent crimes and voted in the 2020 election," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis exclusively told Fox News Digital on Friday. ICE ARRESTS PERUVIAN NATIONAL ACCUSED OF ILLEGALLY VOTING IN 2024 ELECTION AS DHS CITES SIMILAR CASES "Any noncitizens who vote illegally in our elections will be arrested and removed. American elections are only for Americans." Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), a division of DHS, confirmed in a statement that Higgs had illegally voted in the 2020 election. FORMER KANSAS MAYOR WHO PLEADED GUILTY TO ILLEGAL VOTING TURNS HIMSELF IN TO ICE HSI’s Atlanta office arrested Higgs in Decatur, Georgia on Sept. 3, and he is currently in the custody of ERO, the ICE subdivision that handles migrant removal operations. Higgs was admitted into the U.S. in October 1976 as a lawful permanent resident – commonly dubbed a green card holder. The Trump DHS has since placed him in proceedings to revoke his immigration status due to his lengthy rap sheet. TRUMP DOJ UNLEASHES LARGEST DENATURALIZATION EFFORT IN DEPARTMENT HISTORY — AND SAYS IT’S ‘ONLY THE BEGINNING’ "This criminal alien from the Bahamas has a rap sheet for multiple violent crimes, including armed robbery, domestic violence, and assault on a police officer," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said. "On top of all of that, he illegally voted in the 2020 election," he added. MORE THAN A QUARTER-MILLION NONCITIZENS MAY BE REGISTERED TO VOTE IN 4 KEY STATES, DHS ALLEGES Higgs’ record also includes resisting arrest, two counts of grand larceny and two counts of possession of a weapon during a violent crime. Of the voting-related charge, Mullin said just one noncitizen casting a ballot is enough to cancel out an American citizen’s vote. "Thanks to the hard work of the men and women of ICE, this criminal will be removed from our country and can never interfere in our elections again," he continued. DHS also provided several other recent cases of illegal immigrants or ineligible voters committing or being charged with election-related crimes. In August, Colombian illegal immigrant Carlos Jaramillo-Grajales was sentenced to three years in prison following an ICE investigation that led to a guilty plea in a case where he was found to have committed identity theft to illegally vote in elections for more than 20 years, according to the agency. "Federal immigration laws serve to safeguard our nation’s borders and protect the integrity of our government," said Gregory Kehoe, U.S. attorney for the Middle District of Florida. "Those who seek to circumvent, exploit, or break these laws will be prosecuted fully," he said in an August statement. In New Jersey, a Slovakian national was found to have illegally voted in the 2022 midterms, according to HSI – which also cited the case of an Australian national accused of illegally casting ballots in both 2022 and 2024 in Louisiana. Mauritanian national Mahady Sacko was busted by an ICE and FBI partnership in Democrat-run Philadelphia, and charged with voter fraud. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Sacko allegedly voted illegally multiple times going back to 2008. He was already under an order of removal, DHS said in a statement, stating that he "exhausted all appeals" and an immigration board upheld his removal order as of 2002 but he remained in the country. articles.title: Top Trump political adviser James Blair says he’s ‘cautiously optimistic’ about midterms
articles.summary: The Republican Party is facing serious headwinds going into November.
articles.body: The Republican Party is facing serious headwinds going into November. The party that controls the White House typically loses seats in Congress in the midterms. On top of that, President Donald Trump’s approval rating has hit a new low, and voters continue to express dissatisfaction with the economy and the war with Iran. Yet James Blair, a top Trump political adviser, said he still believes Republicans can hang on to their majorities in Congress — although he knows it won’t be easy. “‘I’m cautiously optimistic,” Blair said. “I won’t predict, you know, how many seats are going to be in either chamber come November. But, I do think there is a path for us to retain both majorities and defy history, for sure.” Blair made his remarks in an interview with “Here’s the Scoop: Election Edition,” NBC News’ new Saturday podcast series hosted by chief White House correspondent Garrett Haake. Listen and follow “Here’s the Scoop: Election Edition” here. Blair served as deputy White House chief of staff until April and has been at the center of Trump’s political operations, now serving as the chief of the president’s MAGA Inc. super PAC. During the campaign, Blair was Trump’s political director and is known for his close relationship with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who served as a campaign manager in 2024. Blair acknowledged that Democrats have some advantages this cycle. But he said he believes this post-Labor Day period is where the “heavy lifting” begins and that Democrats may see their polling advantages slip. Comparing Democratic candidates to unpopular members of their party, like Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Blair added, is a strategy he hopes GOP candidates will use. He said he views this year’s midterms as being driven by both national and local concerns. “There is a national backdrop against which things are being fought, and there are local considerations and sort of very specific considerations that a good campaign will be able to utilize both of,” he said. “What they [Democrats] want a Republican to be measured against is, ‘Do you think everything is going perfectly?’” Blair said. “Our candidates, the challenge for them is to not be measured against the measuring stick the Democrats lay out for them, but to be measured against their opposition.” On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance echoed Blair’s message at a private breakfast in Dallas for Republicans from battleground states. “We’ve got to nationalize this election,” he said. “We’ve got to talk about all the crazy things the Democrats are doing.” Addressing dissatisfaction on Iran and the economy Blair’s comments come as voters’ views of Trump have sunk this year. An NBC News Decision Desk Poll this month found that just 36% of U.S. adults approve of the way Trump is handling his job as president. On Trump’s handling of the Iran war, those polled scored the president even lower, with just 31% expressing approval. Blair downplayed concerns about the war, saying that polling he’s seen has shown voters have begun to care less about the issue. “As things have settled down and people see that we’re in control and are coming in for a landing, you’re seeing numbers with the voters that are sensitive to that moving back in the Republicans’ direction,” he said. “We saw that over the summer around the MOU [memorandum of understanding signed between the U.S. and Iran], and again, settling again as there’s not been, sort of, daily action.” Earlier this week, the U.S. and Iran traded strikes, with the U.S. military hitting five Iranian oil tankers after Iran struck two U.S. warships. On Wednesday, the president told Republicans gathered in Dallas for a GOP midterm convention that the war with Iran would not end until after Election Day. Trump has repeatedly said that the ongoing conflict has achieved its goal of preventing Iran from building a nuclear weapon, something that Blair cited as a political success, despite the president’s low marks from voters on his handling of the war. “The president made a correct decision in the scope of history to solve a problem that has been bipartisan-agreed as a problem for 47 years in this country,” he said. “I think we can manage our way through, in September and October, to still be successful, and I think we will be.” Another area where voters give the president low marks is on the economy and inflation. An August Reuters/Ipsos poll found that just 32% of registered voters approved of the president’s handling of the economy. In that same poll, a slightly higher share of voters — 37% — said they believed the Democratic Party had a better plan, policy or approach to the economy than the share who said so about Republicans, 36%. Blair downplayed concerns that views of the economy could cost the GOP its control of Congress, arguing that the president and Republican leaders were still dealing with inflation left over from President Joe Biden, who left the White House in January 2025. “We’re still cleaning up that mess, and we need more time to finish the job,” Blair said. “That’s what we’re asking for in November.” That message of asking for patience was reflected at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas this week. “All of the price hikes that happened under Biden that were caused by their policies don’t just immediately drop,” Blair added. In February 2025, the first full month of Trump’s second term, inflation was 2.8% year over year. It dipped as low as 2.4% in April 2025, the month Trump announced his “Liberation Day” tariff regime — but before those tariffs had taken effect. Fast-forward 18 months, and both tariffs and the Iran war energy crisis have helped push inflation back up to 3.4% as of August. Trump ‘on the ballot’ In recent weeks, the president has increasingly focused on the midterms, telling reporters that he plans to travel and campaign in 35 races. He has also asked supporters to “pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” an idea that Blair embraced. “Democrats are already using him as a turnout tool for their voters, whether Republicans do that or not. So that’s sort of baked into the cake,” Blair said. “The other side’s already going to, you know, attack however they’re going to attack, do whatever they think they can do to motivate their voters to win. We want to use all of the tools at our disposal to help our voters.” Specifically, Blair pointed to low-propensity male voters, or those who don’t vote in every election, as ones whom Trump may be uniquely able to encourage to go to the polls. He used an example of a voter who “works 40 to 60 hours a week, is not super engaged in politics. … He’s not watching this podcast. He’s not watching the news. He’s not trying to be engaged in politics on a regular basis.” “That’s a guy who voted in the presidential race, but, historically he’s not voted in the midterms because that’s just the nature of those voters,” Blair added. “So for the president to lay out the stakes to that individual to give him a reason to come out and vote that transcends, you know, not just what he’s hearing from his local candidates, but sort of broadens out the picture nationally and what the stakes are, I think that’s very useful.” Still, Blair said he doesn’t expect the same coalition that sent Trump back to the White House in 2024 to align with the president again this year. “Coalitions are never exactly the same,” he said, adding: “Maybe a coalition’s core sticks, and then every election is a little different.” He pointed specifically to Latino voters, who voted for the Republican nominee in 2024 in record numbers. “Do I think that Republicans generically will get the same percentage with Hispanics in ‘26 as they did in ‘24? You know, probably not,” Blair said. “But will Hispanics still overperform for Republicans, you know, in broad, relative to where they did in 2018 and 2022? Yes, I think that’s likely.” How Latinos vote this fall could be a significant factor in how many seats Texas Republicans and California Democrats win after redrawing their congressional maps. For example, Republicans’ three top targets in Texas — the 28th, 34th and 35th districts — are all overwhelmingly Latino districts. If the president’s standing with Latino voters wanes, that could jeopardize Republicans’ ability to win these seats. MAGA Inc. begins to unload its coffers Blair also spoke about the role that MAGA Inc. will have in the midterms. At the end of July, when its most recent campaign finance disclosure was filed, the group had a war chest of more than $400 million. Asked about some Republicans’ concerns that Trump may not choose to spend the bulk of the MAGA Inc. cash before Election Day, Blair said simply, “I can assure that the president will leave it all on the field to keep his majorities.” Over the summer, some members of the GOP were particularly concerned about Texas, where state Attorney General Ken Paxton ousted Sen. John Cornyn in a bruising Republican primary. Paxton had Trump’s endorsement, but much of the Republican Party backed Cornyn, known as a strong fundraiser with a record of winning in the state. Public polling has indicated a close, competitive race between Paxton and Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, who has led the state attorney general in fundraising. On Saturday, MAGA Inc. booked $10 million worth of TV ad time in the state. Blair dismissed concerns about Paxton’s strength in the race, saying, “The fact is Ken Paxton had $100 million spent against him in the primary. Talarico had $0 spent against him in the primary, and that has an impact on candidate images that takes time to rectify. But the resources … have begun to be deployed now in earnest [and] will take care of that problem.” On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that MAGA Inc. was funneling $49 million through a new group — No Going Back PAC — that would run TV ads in Senate races across the country. Blair didn’t detail the group’s spending plans, but acknowledged a widening battlefield of competitive statewide races, including in Alaska’s Senate race, where former Rep. Mary Peltola is the Democratic nominee running against Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The race is complicated by the presence of a third candidate, also a Republican named Dan Sullivan. (In Alaska, the top four candidates in the primary, regardless of party, advance to the ranked-choice general election.) Republicans have accused Democrats of sowing confusion among voters by recruiting Dan J. Sullivan to run as a spoiler in the race against the senator, Dan S. Sullivan. “We know that national Democrats did that,” Blair said, without pointing to specific evidence. “We know that the press release for that candidate was written by a consultant to Mary Peltola. No one even disputes this fact. That is rigging a process using ranked-choice voting against the people of Alaska.” Democrats have not taken credit for recruiting Dan J. Sullivan, a teacher, into the race. Blair acknowledged that his presence and Peltola’s past electoral success in the state are making the race close. “I don’t dispute that’s a competitive race,” he said. “Mary Peltola’s been elected statewide before. We know this. So I mean, I think for us, like, we’re smart enough to read numbers. We know where things are. We’re going to fish where the fish are, and we’re gonna go try to win the majority, you know, protect the majority in all these places.”

articles.body:
President Trump’s pledge to give $5,000 to every U.S. adult if Republicans keep control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections has raised questions over whether the plan could cross legal lines.

Trump announced the dividends on the first night of the Republican National Committee (RNC) midterm convention in Dallas Wednesday night.

Those on the right and left has expressed their concerns on how Trump’s dividends would work, given the federal government would have to send out an estimated $1.2 trillion, according to The Hill’s Sophie Brams.

South Carolina Rep. Ralph Norman (R) was among those in the GOP to speak out against the idea, saying on the social platform X he had “serious concerns” about the plan.

With the midterm elections less than two months away, Trump will head to battleground North Carolina to campaign with GOP Senate nominee Michael Whatley on Wednesday.

Unlike Whatley, other candidates are choosing to keep Trump at an arm’s length, according to The Hill’s Julia Manchester.

Trump is in Ireland this weekend and met with Irish President Catherine Connolly and Taoiseach Micheál Martin.

articles.title: El-Sayed’s ISNA appearance draws scrutiny over controversial speakers
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed appeared on an ISNA panel with Cenk Uygur and Zaid Shakir days before the 9/11 anniversary, raising new questions about his campaign.
articles.body: Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is facing questions about his appearance at an Islamic Society of North America (ISNA) convention after the organization removed a Pakistani cleric from its lineup following scrutiny of his past remarks about Hitler, Jews and jihad. Mufti Tariq Masood had been scheduled to speak at ISNA's annual convention last week in Detroit alongside El-Sayed. The Washington Free Beacon first reported that ISNA had quietly pulled Masood from its list of speakers last month. This came after his past comments, including remarks appearing to praise Hitler's persecution of the Jews and defending child marriage, sparked backlash against ISNA. Dr. Andrew Bostom, who reviewed one of Masood's sermons, told Fox News Digital that the cleric "basically said that the Quran had foreshadowed Hitler 1,400 years ago." FATWAS, HOLY WARS AND SOCIALISM: INSIDE THE ISLAMIC CONFERENCE WHERE EL-SAYED DREW A HERO’S WELCOME Bostom said that Masood's remarks should not be looked at in isolation, but rather within a larger pattern of antisemitic themes that have appeared in writings of some Muslim scholars. He cited Muhammad Sayyid Tantawy, the late grand imam of Al-Azhar University in Egypt, who he said was "the near papal equivalent for Sunni Islam," in terms of his influence. The controversy over Masood prompted the Zionist Organization of America (ZOA) to ask Secretary of State Marco Rubio to deny or review any visa issued to the cleric. "Masood is a racist, Jew-hate-mongering, anti-American, anti-British, conspiracy-promoting, murder- and terror-inciter. Masood even praises Hitler’s genocide of Jews as doing the right thing, similar to the Quran’s instructions," ZOA National President Morton Klein wrote in his Aug. 19 letter to Rubio. At the time, Bostom said it was unclear whether Masood had already entered the U.S. or still planned to attend the convention, even if he had been removed from the list of speakers. TIM SCOTT GOES SCORCHED EARTH ON EL-SAYED: 'HE'S FOR HAMAS, BUT HE'S AGAINST AMERICA' While Masood ultimately did not speak at the convention, his removal from the lineup did not resolve questions about the event's speakers or El-Sayed's decision to participate. At the conference, El-Sayed appeared on a panel with far-left Young Turks founder Cenk Uygur and controversial New Jersey-based cleric Zaid Shakir, according to ISNA's itinerary. The panel was titled "Cultivating God Awareness in a Turmoiled America." In its description, ISNA said the session was aimed at turning taqwa, which means God-awareness, "into actionable guidance, equipping participants not merely to survive but thrive in workplaces, schools, digital spaces, and community life, and to succeed on their own terms." CBS CHIEF BARI WEISS' INVOLVEMENT IN VIRAL EL-SAYED REPORT SPARKS DEBATE AMONG CRITICS Neither Uygur nor Shakir are strangers to controversy. In February, Uygur wrote on X, "I no longer believe the official 9/11 story." Uygur said that those who would be outraged by his statement had been "brainwashed by corporate media." Shakir has described himself as "extremely anti-American," according to The Washington Free Beacon. The outlet also reported that in 1992, Shakir urged Muslims to embrace "extrasystemic political action," including "noncooperation tactics to guerrilla war" to influence government policies. The ISNA conference took place just days before the 25th anniversary of 9/11, making Uygur and Shakir's presence, and El-Sayed's participation, all the more notable. El-Sayed faced his own 9/11 controversy earlier this week over now-deleted tweets from 2021 in which he said he mourned the lives lost in the attacks before taking a swipe at America, according to The New York Post. "Today, I mourn the 3K lives, 6K injuries, & infrastructural devastation in NYC, perpetrated ignorantly in the name of my faith. Tomorrow, I’ll mourn ~1M lives, millions of injuries, & infrastructural devastation in 3 countries, perpetrated ignorantly in the name of my country," El-Sayed wrote on Sept. 11, 2021. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE While addressing the ISNA conference, El-Sayed reportedly focused on anti-Muslim hate, according to the Post. "We found ourselves in a moment now where, as people point to us, Muslim Americans, they want to tell us that we don’t belong," El-Sayed said, according to the Post. "They want to tell us that this country is not ours. They want to tell us that because of our names or how we pray, that somehow we are less than," he added. El-Sayed previously faced scrutiny for campaigning alongside controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who is Uygur's nephew. Piker was criticized back in 2019 for saying that "America deserved 9/11." He later apologized and retracted the statement. El-Sayed has offered criticism of some of Piker's remarks but has yet to fully disavow him. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed and ISNA for comment.

articles.title: The dangerous evolution of Gavin Newsom
articles.summary: Often called a “political chameleon,” Newsom seems to be morphing into the actual species that evolved to adjust to its environment.
articles.body:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) wants you to know that he is evolving.

Newsom is facing a rising radical movement among Democrats, including a surging contingent aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America. He is struggling in polls and therefore eager to show the skill identified by Darwin that allows certain species to thrive in their environment: adaptation.

Newsom has recently declared capitalism a failure. He is now joining his competitors for president in offering up the Supreme Court and its independence to the far left. His free fall into rage politics is a cautionary tale for those who want to return the Democratic Party to more centrist positions.

Often called a “political chameleon,” Newsom seems to be morphing into the actual species that evolved to adjust to its environment, including more nimble feet.

Although natural selection takes place over many years and even eons, Newsom does not have the luxury of time. He does not want to be eliminated by the more politically fit opponents to his left.

Polls continue to show he receives more media support than public support. He trails Kamala Harris by 15 points in recent polling and is nearly tied with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

Harris and Buttigieg quickly turned their backs on the norms governing the Supreme Court to support court-packing. Harris dismissed those of us in opposition as engaging in mere “ nostalgia .”

Newsom had previously tried to offer a sane alternative to these voices. But he has now found himself their quiet companion in a primal scream session. As he began to vanish in political polling, he decided he would not be outcrazied by Democratic opponents.

With candidates like Texas’s Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico calling for the “dismantling” of capitalism as an “oppressive system,” Newsom finds himself needing to cater to the mob. He has now declared that “nostalgia is not working” while adding that “capitalism as we know it doesn’t work either.”

Newsom has recently been campaigning in blue states such as New Hampshire, repeating his mantra that capitalism as “not working.”

But these days, it is not enough for socialists and the far left merely to oppose the most successful economic system in the history of the world. Newsom was still being labeled as an establishment politician. So he tried to dispel that impression with his signature toothy grin and astonished demeanor, claiming that he is really undermining the system from within as “ an established insurgent .”

Again, that is not enough for the current political environment. So this week, he changed his position on the Supreme Court, to say that he is now “open” to court-packing.

Packing the court is considered essential today for any viable Democratic candidate. Some are openly calling for the imposition of a litmus test for all candidates: As they put it, it is a choice between “ packed or sacked .”

Even moderate figures such as Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) have now yielded to the mob in expressing a willingness to pack the Supreme Court.

So Newsom wants the far left to know that he is yet again evolving: “My initial instinct — me, a year ago, I would have said no out of concern that it will continue to be expanded. … I’m finding myself evolving on it.”

The question is what Newsom and his Democrat opponents will offer next in their political adaptation. These candidates have shown that no institution or value is more important than their securing power. At this rate, we will be fortunate to have anything more than the ship itself after the race to toss institutions and “nostalgic” values over the side.

The danger for Newsom — like the danger of any fast-tracking of evolution — is that the environment can change, leaving you with an adaptation that makes you even more likely to be eliminated. Newsom knows that attacking our constitutional or economic systems will not play well in the general election, but he also knows he will never see the 2028 general election if his opponents on the left outflank him.

Moreover, offerings like the Supreme Court or our economic system are unlikely to satiate the far left. As I discuss in “ Rage and the Republic ,” history shows that establishment figures rarely survive the mob politics they seek to use for their own advantage.

In the meantime, because of the cynical calculations of leaders like Newsom, we face a growing threat of doing lasting harm to our constitutional system. The framers warned us of these voices of “mobocracy” that would tear apart the contemporary revolution in France, which became known as “the Terror.”

The danger is that, while the majority opposes court packing and socialism, the new majority in Congress could force changes without amending the Constitution. That certainly can be done with court packing. Once a new liberal majority is secured, there would then be little barrier to achieving many of the objectives of a radical agenda long discussed by professors and pundits . Some have argued that, with control of the court and radical constitutional changes, Republicans will not be able to win another election.

In other words, the radicals hope to change the environment to prevent further adaptation and future competition.

Kurt Vonnegut once said, “Evolution can go to hell as far as I am concerned. What a mistake we are.” After watching the chameleonic Gavin Newsom, it seems that we may be on the cusp of precisely such an evolutionary mistake.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of “ Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution. “

articles.title: New bill would restrict SNAP benefits in 9 states. Here’s what could be cut
articles.summary: A new law introduced in the House this month would add more restrictions to what types of food SNAP recipients can buy with their monthly benefits.
articles.body:
Related video above: SNAP error rates could change benefits

(NEXSTAR) – A new law introduced in the House this month would add more restrictions to what types of food SNAP recipients can buy with their monthly benefits.

The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) helps about 37 million Americans buy food, mostly in the form of groceries. But in nine states, some SNAP beneficiaries who have a hard time preparing fresh food for themselves can also use their EBT cards to buy hot meals from approved restaurants.

A new bill, introduced by Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) , would eliminate that option.

The bill would eliminate SNAP’s Restaurant Meals Program (RMP), which states can opt in to. The program is meant to help people who can’t easily cook, or don’t have permanent housing, get access to food.

California, one of the select states where the Restaurant Meals Program is currently operating , says RMP targets “people that are a high risk for chronic hunger,” like those with disabilities or the homeless.

Not everyone can sign up for RMP and not every restaurant is an approved vendor. In order to qualify, SNAP recipients must be either elderly, disabled, homeless or the spouse of an RMP participant.

Only nine states have currently operating Restaurant Meals Programs, according to the USDA: Arizona, California, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, New York, Rhode Island and Virginia.

The bill, titled “Ending Restaurant Purchases with SNAP Act of 2026,” would amend federal law to cut the program entirely. Rep. Gill described RMP as a “loophole” that allows federal benefits to be spent on unhealthy food.

“SNAP is supposed to help struggling Americans put nutritious food on the table, not stick taxpayers with the bill for fast food,” Rep. Gill said in a statement to Newsweek . “More than half a billion dollars in SNAP benefits have gone to restaurants through this loophole in just two years while the Trump administration is working to get junk food out of the program. My bill ends this ridiculous loophole and makes sure SNAP dollars are used for what the program was created to do: help Americans afford nutritious groceries.”

The second Trump administration has placed increasing focus on what types of food SNAP dollars can and can’t purchase as part of its push to “Make America Healthy Again.” Twenty-three states had been granted waivers to bar SNAP recipients from spending the federal dollars on things like soda, energy drinks and candy before a judge struck down the new restrictions in June.

Critics say the added restrictions unnecessarily stigmatizes the food choices of low-income Americans.

“It’s an opportunity to say you’re doing something, while really just stigmatizing a single group of people for choices that everybody in America really makes,” Chris Bernard of Hunger Free Oklahoma told Nexstar’s KFOR .

A different approach has been proposed in the “ Fresh Bucks for Fresh Produce ” Act, introduced in Congress in July. The legislation would establish a pilot program granting households an extra $60 a month that could only be spent on fruit or vegetables.

Both bills have been referred to the House Committee on Agriculture for consideration.

articles.body:
President Trump asked the Smithsonian Institution in late Friday social media posts to install a 30-foot-tall statue of George Washington outside of its National Museum of American History (NMAH) and open an exhibit to honor the founding father.

The president requested that the museum complex replace the “Infinity” statue, which has stood outside of the NMAH since 1967, with one depicting the nation’s first president.

“That strange modernist sculpture tells visitors nothing about America, inspires no one, and honors none of our Great American Heroes,” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

“George Washington does,” he continued. “He is easily America’s Greatest Hero. Without him, our Country and our Freedoms wouldn’t exist.”

Trump asked for work on the proposed, five-year exhibit to begin “now,” adding he wants to be open through Feb. 22, 2032 — the 300th anniversary of Washington’s birthday.

The president has repeatedly criticized Smithsonian leadership for promoting a “social justice” agenda and sought to direct changes to museum exhibits.

The Smithsonian operates independent of the White House, but its leadership is overseen by a Board of Regents — includes Vice President Vance, Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, bipartisan lawmakers and a group of citizens.

This week, Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch announced he would step down from his role by the end of the year amid disputes with the Trump administration.

In July, Trump directed the installation of signage outside of the NMAH to warn visitors that some of the museum’s exhibits did not match his administration’s perspective on the nation’s past.

The president cited a July White House report that criticized Smithsonian leaders as “extreme” activists and concluded the NMAH “fails in the basic task of illuminating” U.S. history in its content.

The Trump administration also referenced this report when they threatened in September to cut federal agencies’ cooperation with the museum complex.

“Instead of focusing on ideological activism, the leaders of America’s taxpayer-funded, National History Museum should be focused on telling America’s story—fairly, accurately, and coherently—and there is no better person to start with than George Washington,” the president wrote in his Saturday Truth Social post.

The Smithsonian Institution did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed touts ‘whole a--’ medical credentials while defending sex changes for children
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed, a Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, argues 'whole a--' doctors should decide trans treatment without government interference.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said the government should not restrict sex changes, arguing that "whole a--" doctors like himself should be allowed to make their own determinations for patients' treatment plans. The remarks came during El-Sayed's Friday rally held at Michigan State University, during which the former Detroit Health Department head responded to a student's question about protecting sex changes. Since launching his campaign, El-Sayed has flaunted that he is a "physician" and, if elected, he would be the first doctor to serve as a Democratic senator in 50 years. However, Fox News Digital previously reported El-Sayed has never held a medical license in Michigan or New York. "I went to a whole a-- medical school, everybody I graduated with also went to whole a-- medical school," El-Sayed said. "And then ... they went to whole a-- residency. Right? And some of them went to whole a-- fellowship. They took whole a-- exams to provide whole a-- healthcare." DEM SENATE HOPEFUL’S ‘PHYSICIAN’ CAMPAIGN PITCH UNDER FIRE AFTER LICENSE RECORDS REVEAL KEY GAPS "They are the experts that a patient wants to see when they seek care," El-Sayed continued. "And the decision about what healthcare is necessary ought to be held between a patient — and or their parents if they're under the age of 18 — and their doctor. That's it." The remarks come as the Trump administration has made major strides in restricting minors' access to "sex-rejecting" procedures, which include hormone therapy and surgeries. Earlier this week, the Justice Department announced that Mount Sinai had joined other hospitals, like Texas Children's Hospital, the Cleveland Clinic Foundation and Connecticut Children's Hospital, to halt sex change procedures for children after reaching an agreement with the Trump administration. MEDICAID ENDS FUNDING FOR CHILD SEX-CHANGE PROCEDURES AS TRUMP ADMIN SLAMS 'EXPERIMENTAL' TREATMENTS El-Sayed has made the promise of Medicare for All — government-run healthcare — as the major selling point of his campaign; he said that even though the government will be covering the bill, it needs to stay out of the doctor's decisions about a patient's treatment plan. "I don't think the government gets to have a say about what health care is provided in what circumstances and why," El-Sayed said. "And to me, that is the standard on which we decide how we make health care decisions." THE MEDICARE FOR ALL TRADE-OFFS SOCIALISTS AREN'T TALKING ABOUT, ACCORDING TO EXPERTS "Not what the government says you can or can't do, but what a patient and/or their parent, if they're under 18, and their provider to decide. That's the most important thing," El-Sayed continued. "And there's a lot of disinformation about us, what we're talking about, when we talk about reproductive rights and when we're talking about health care for the trans folks. But, in the end, the place where the rubber meets the rope is in that clinical room between a patient and a provider, and that to me is the center we should engage on." El-Sayed argued that Republicans agree with his belief that treatment decisions should be between a patient and their doctor, pointing to the Right to Try Act, which allows terminally ill patients to try experimental drug treatments that aren't yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration after they have exhausted all other treatment options. "Because conservatives fought for a very long time for this legislation called 'Right to Try' legislation, which is the idea that the government couldn't tell you [that] you couldn't have a certain medication," El-Sayed said. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROBE COULD UPEND WIDELY USED TRANSGENDER YOUTH TREATMENT GUIDELINES "So they agree that the decision about healthcare ought to be between the person and their provider. That's it. So let's use that standard, and keep to that standard, and make sure the government doesn't have the ability to tell you what you can or cannot do with your own life," El-Sayed said. However, the research on the efficacy of treating individuals with gender dysphoria by allowing them to change sexes with "cross-sex" hormones and puberty blockers is limited. The World Professional Association for Transgender Health, whose guidelines are used by leading medical associations like the American Academy of Peditatrics, is currently facing a lawsuit from the Federal Trade Commission stemming from allegations that its guidelines misled parents about the "medical consensus and medical necessity, as well as the safety and effectiveness" of sex change procedures. The FTC has accused WPATH of failing to disclose the side effects associated with some procedures, such as patients experiencing incontinence, erectile pain, mood disturbances, pelvic pain, and vaginal pain stemming from "cross-sex" hormones. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Meanwhile, countries that have socialized medicine have put restrictions in place for minors' seeking sex changes. In England, the National Health Service put a pause on "cross-sex" hormones for 16- and 17-year-olds in March after finding research was "really weak" to support it. The country already had a ban in place restricting children under 16 years old from taking sex-change hormones. El-Sayed's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment regarding his medical credentials.

articles.title: $25 million in national park project funds blocked by Trump administration: Report
articles.summary: The Trump administration has reportedly blocked more than 130 planned projects at national parks across the country, putting more than $25 million worth of funding on hold. The Interior Department, which oversees the National Park Service (NPS), “disapproved” of agreements last month for projects at Yellowstone, Yosemite, Zion, Joshua Tree and other parks, The Washington…
articles.body:
The Trump administration has reportedly blocked more than 130 planned projects at national parks across the country, putting more than $25 million worth of funding on hold.

The Interior Department, which oversees the National Park Service (NPS), “disapproved” of agreements last month for projects at Yellowstone, Yosemite, Zion, Joshua Tree and other parks, The Washington Post reported, citing internal documents.

NPS often works with outside organizations for projects that require additional workers or specialized expertise rather than hiring additional federal employees, the Post added.

The outlet reported that the funding came from sources including congressional appropriations and existing federal programs and was awaiting the Interior’s approval before it could be released.

Interior spokesperson Aubrie Spady confirmed to The Washington Post that the department had rejected agreements with groups she described as “actively working against the best interests of the American people and the priorities of this administration.”

“This decisive action is ensuring that these taxpayer dollars are being used in alignment with the administration’s objectives to make life more affordable for Americans, unleash domestic energy production and expand access to our public lands,” she said.

Joshua Tree National Park in California was reportedly the most impacted, with at least 10 projects blocked, including wildfire preparation, burned area restoration and the removal of rodents that carry hantavirus from historic buildings.

Internal documents warned that losing funding for the projects could make it more difficult and costly to fight fires at the park.

“If this work is not completed, the park will be unable to fight wildfire. Fires will be larger and fire suppression will be more expensive,” the documents read, according to the Post.

Other projects would have worked to protect prehistoric Native American mounds in Iowa from falling trees, supported efforts to preserve an endangered snake species in California and paid for the care of sled dogs at Denali National Park and Preserve in Alaska.

The Great Basin Institute, a conservation nonprofit that works with federal land agencies, reportedly had more than 70 agreements worth at least $12 million rejected.

The group’s CEO, Peter Woodruff, told the Post that it was not directly notified by the Interior about the decision and did not know why its agreements had been blocked.

In July, President Trump notably signed orders reducing the size of Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments in Utah, prompting Patagonia and a coalition of Native American and environmental groups to challenge the reductions in court.

articles.title: 25 years after the anthrax attacks, we are still unprepared for biological warfare
articles.summary: When the nation desperately needs help, it will be from a government that has lost the ability to provide it.
articles.body:
In the early, chaotic days after the Sept. 11, 2001 terror attacks, five letters were dropped into a mailbox in Princeton, New Jersey, across from the Princeton University campus. Containing a coarse brown powder later identified as anthrax spores, the envelopes were addressed to media organizations, including NBC News and the New York Post.

By early October 2001, the phones inside New York City’s emergency operations center were ringing off the hook with demands for Cipro , the antibiotic used to prevent anthrax infection after exposure. Powerful politicians and government officials were calling. I remember the menace in one personal assistant’s voice: “The senator wants his Cipro. Now.”

They believed, with perfect conviction, that they were entitled to receive it first — and that I was the one keeping it from them. It got ugly fast.

I have often thought about those calls over the last 25 years, and here is what they taught me. Fear is a solvent. Firm convictions about masks and social distancing and vaccine safety dissolve when people believe that they, or their children, could die. Upon first contact with a deadly pathogen, Americans will not be divided over whether they want protection. They will be unanimous. But right now, there is nobody to provide it.

COVID-19 should have pulled us together, but it did just the opposite. Instead of learning the lessons and building back stronger, we spent the last six years pointing fingers at the institutions of government, as the institutions themselves have come apart. That is the perfect storm we have built. When the nation desperately needs help, it will be from a government that has lost the ability to provide it.

With her latest book, Annie Jacobsen shines a spotlight on this alarming vulnerability. “ Biological War ” takes a threat we all agreed to ignore and lays it out in riveting detail: the Soviet stockpiles of engineered pathogens, built to kill hundreds of millions in a matter of days; the proliferation of bioweapons labs around the world, creating yet more novel pathogens through high risk “gain of function” research.

The book is not alarmism; it is dispassionate reporting based on dozens of interviews with high-level political, governmental, medical and military experts. Its conclusions should stop us cold. The weapons to end civilization exist, they are more available than they have ever been, and the geopolitical environment has never been more conducive to their use.

The good news is that we don’t need a miracle to stop a pandemic; we just need epidemiologists to do their vital work — finding the sick and tracing their contacts to break the chain of transmission. Nothing more exotic than trained people, funded and in place before the first case appears.

The COVID crisis revealed major gaps in our ability to do this. Over the past 18 months we have shut down the U.S. Agency for International Development and proposed cutting the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s budget. We walked out of the World Health Organization in January, surrendering our seat at the table where the world’s disease surveillance data is shared.

Here is the part that keeps me awake. No level of government could support the population at the speed and scale a major biological attack would demand. Not just to treat the sick, but to feed the people who cannot leave their homes, and to rapidly dispense preventive medications — oral antibiotics for anthrax or plague — through local points of dispensing.

We possess extraordinary scientific, medical, pharmaceutical research and logistics capabilities, but capabilities are not preparedness. Preparedness is capability organized for action, at speed, under pressure. That requires national coordination. The Federal Emergency Management Agency, the agency charged with this, has been cut, second-guessed and floated for relocation.

That is the agency Cameron Hamilton now inherits. His recent confirmation ends a long period of temporary leadership. Now he must be given the resources to build and the authority to act. This means a funded FEMA and a clear mission. It means public health and emergency management planning together before the event instead of in the middle of one. And it means the new administrator putting his agency in the room where biological threats are being tracked — not waiting to be invited after the outbreak has a name.

Call it civil defense. Call it whatever you want. We need a national effort — a sustained, funded, unglamorous program to rebuild stockpiles, strengthen disease surveillance and refresh and validate mass-prophylaxis plans.

Twenty-five years ago next week, a handful of envelopes sent people scrambling for protection. The next biological emergency will move faster, reach farther and demand infinitely more from the institutions charged with protecting us.

The threat is real. The system is blinking red. We need to be ready when the phones start ringing.

Kelly McKinney served as associate commissioner at the Department of Health during New York City’s response to the 2001 anthrax attacks and later as deputy commissioner of the New York City Office of Emergency Management.

articles.title: The one line from JD Vance’s GOP keynote that reveals his vision for America
articles.summary: JD Vance framed the midterm elections as a fight over every American child's birthright in a Dallas keynote that previewed his post-Trump GOP vision.
articles.body: Vice President JD Vance used his keynote address at the Republican midterm convention Thursday to frame the November elections as a fight over America’s future, arguing that every child is entitled to inherit the country’s opportunities regardless of background. The speech also gave Vance one of his most prominent national platforms since becoming vice president to define his own political vision, as he emerges as a central figure in the GOP’s post-Trump future and speculation continues about a potential 2028 presidential campaign. "Every American child is born an heir, born with the right to inherit the blessings of the greatest country on Earth — not because of who their parents are, what they look like or where they come from, but because they are Americans and this is our country," Vance said in Dallas. "And that birthright, ladies and gentlemen, is what this November is all about," he added. VANCE, CRUZ, HEAD TO IOWA ON 2026 MISSIONS AS 2028 GOP RACE TO SUCCEED TRUMP HEATS UP Vance tied that idea to his own family, speaking about the birth of his fourth child, Alec, six weeks ago. He said he wants his son and all American children to grow up with access to clean water, healthy food, a quality education, safe communities and the opportunity to afford a home and raise a family. He also connected that vision to the legacy of his late friend Charlie Kirk, who was killed one year ago. Vance said Kirk encouraged young men to fall in love, start families and become fathers. The speech marked a shift from the personal story of Vance’s Appalachian upbringing that he emphasized during the 2024 Republican convention. Instead, Vance presented himself as a father focused on the country his children will inherit, while using the platform to preview the issues and themes that could define his future in the Republican Party. TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE Vance then pivoted from his family-focused message to a sweeping attack on the Democratic Party. He accused Democrats of abandoning working-class Americans and becoming increasingly hostile toward the country’s traditional values. "The Democrats are the party of hatred," Vance said. "They’re the party that despises America and the people who built it." FOLLOW FOX NEWS DIGITAL’S COVERAGE OF THE GOP’S 2026 MIDTERM CONVENTION He urged Republicans to view the November election as more than a traditional partisan contest. "This November is so much more than red team versus blue team," Vance said. "It’s about fighting for our fellow citizens, for their dreams, and for the inheritance of a great nation that all of us are going to leave behind." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The speech placed family, faith and national identity at the center of Vance’s midterm message while offering a glimpse of how he could define himself within the Republican Party beyond President Donald Trump.

articles.title: Graham accepts debate with Andrews after challenger pushes for more
articles.summary: Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) announced Friday she plans to debate her Democratic challenger in South Carolina’s Senate race, pediatrician Annie Andrews, ahead of November’s elections. “I’m in,” Graham wrote in a social media post. “On October 11, I will take the debate stage and expose Annie Andrews’ radical positions she’s spent the last year hiding…
articles.body:
Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) announced Friday she plans to debate her Democratic challenger in South Carolina’s Senate race, pediatrician Annie Andrews, ahead of November’s elections.

“I’m in,” Graham wrote in a social media post . “On October 11, I will take the debate stage and expose Annie Andrews’ radical positions she’s spent the last year hiding from South Carolina families.”

“This is your seat, South Carolina, and it will be my honor to show you why I am ready to continue serving you and representing our conservative values in Washington,” she continued.

South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster (R) tapped Graham to fill out the remainder of her brother Lindsey Graham’s Senate term after his death in July . President Trump quickly backed the late senator’s sister for a full term.

In the state’s Republican primary runoff in August, Graham beat Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) to become the GOP’s nominee in this race.

The Oct. 11 event, hosted by local public broadcaster SCETV, will mark Graham’s first public debate since her primary face-off with Norman last month. The appearance caused some to doubt the incumbent’s qualifications after she flubbed a national security question about Taiwan and the South China Sea.

“I’m just going to be honest here … I’m not that informed on national security,” Graham responded, before adding, “But I do support the military.”

Andrews, who has repeatedly challenged the Republican nominee to participate in a debate, responded to Graham’s announcement on Friday evening.

“Darline’s primary debate performance left voters with serious questions about whether she is prepared for this job,” the Democrat said in a statement shared on social media.

“Voters deserve to see us side by side and judge for themselves,” she continued. “I’m eager to finally see Darline on the campaign trail and show South Carolinians exactly why I’m the best person to fight for them in the United States Senate.”

Andrews previously launched an unsuccessful bid for the U.S. House in 2022. The Cook Political Report , a nonpartisan election forecaster, rates South Carolina’s Senate race as “Solid Republican.” The state’s voters supported Trump in the past three presidential elections.
